disease.name: Asthma

overview.description: Asthma is a chronic inflammatory disease of the airways (bronchi) in the lungs. The airways become swollen and narrow, making it difficult to breathe. It is a long-term condition that can be managed but not cured.
overview.age_group: All age groups; often starts in childhood

types.name: Allergic Asthma (Extrinsic)
types.description: Triggered by allergens such as pollen, dust mites, pet dander, or mold. Most common type.

types.name: Non-Allergic Asthma (Intrinsic)
types.description: Not triggered by allergens. Caused by stress, exercise, cold air, smoke, or infections.

types.name: Exercise-Induced Bronchoconstriction (EIB)
types.description: Triggered by physical activity. Airways narrow during or after exercise.

types.name: Occupational Asthma
types.description: Caused by workplace irritants such as chemicals, dust, gases, or fumes.
types.common_in: Adults in industrial or chemical work environments

types.name: Cough-Variant Asthma
types.description: Main symptom is persistent dry cough, with little to no wheezing or shortness of breath.

types.name: Nocturnal Asthma
types.description: Symptoms worsen at night due to hormonal changes, lying down position, or dust mites in bedding.

types.name: Severe Asthma
types.description: Does not respond well to standard treatments. Requires advanced therapy.

types.name: Aspirin-Exacerbated Respiratory Disease (AERD)
types.description: Asthma triggered by aspirin or NSAIDs combined with nasal polyps.

genetic_factors: Family history of asthma or allergies
Atopy (genetic tendency to develop allergic diseases)
Gene mutations related to immune response (ORMDL3, GSDMB, IL-4, IL-13)
environmental_triggers: Allergens: pollen, dust mites, pet dander, cockroach droppings, mold spores
Air pollution: smoke, smog, vehicle exhaust
Occupational chemicals: latex, flour dust, animal proteins

primary_symptoms.name: Wheezing
primary_symptoms.description: A high-pitched whistling sound when breathing, especially during exhalation.
primary_symptoms.onset: During or after exposure to triggers

primary_symptoms.name: Shortness of Breath (Dyspnea)
primary_symptoms.description: Feeling of not being able to get enough air or breathlessness.
primary_symptoms.onset: During exertion or at rest in severe cases

primary_symptoms.name: Chest Tightness
primary_symptoms.description: A squeezing or pressure sensation in the chest.
primary_symptoms.onset: Often early morning or at night

primary_symptoms.name: Chronic Cough
primary_symptoms.description: Persistent cough, especially at night or early morning. May produce mucus.
primary_symptoms.onset: Night or early morning; after exercise

secondary_symptoms: Difficulty sleeping due to breathing issues
Neck muscles visibly strained when breathing
Bluish tint to lips or fingernails (cyanosis — severe/emergency)
warning_signs_of_attack: No improvement after using rescue inhaler
Peak flow reading below 50% personal best
symptoms_in_children: Frequent coughing, especially during play or at night
Wheezing or whistling sound when breathing
Shortness of breath or rapid breathing
Repeated episodes of bronchitis or pneumonia

medical_history: Family history of asthma or allergies
physical_examination: Listening to lungs with stethoscope for wheezing
Observing breathing rate and chest expansion

diagnostic_tests.description: Measures lung function — specifically FEV1 and FVC to detect airflow obstruction.
Measures how fast air can be exhaled using a peak flow meter.
Spirometry before and after bronchodilator use.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Confirms reversible airway obstruction typical of asthma

diagnostic_tests.description: Inhaling methacholine to trigger mild airway narrowing.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Diagnoses asthma when spirometry is normal

diagnostic_tests.description: Skin prick test or blood test (IgE levels) to identify allergens.
Imaging of lungs to rule out other conditions.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Excludes pneumonia, COPD, or other lung disease

diagnostic_tests.description: Complete blood count and total IgE levels.
Non-invasive measurement of blood oxygen saturation.

medicines.note: All medications should be taken only under the supervision of a licensed physician. Self-medication can be dangerous.

categories.purpose: Quick relief during asthma attacks by relaxing airway muscles

medicines.name: Levosalbutamol (Levalbuterol)
medicines.use_case: Acute relief with fewer cardiovascular side effects

categories.purpose: Reduce airway inflammation and prevent asthma symptoms
categories.onset: Several days to weeks for full effect

categories.purpose: Sustained bronchodilation, always used with ICS

medicines.name: Formoterol (Eformoterol)
medicines.use_case: Maintenance and acute symptom relief (SMART therapy)

medicines.name: Budesonide + Formoterol
medicines.use_case: MART / SMART therapy — maintenance and rescue

categories.purpose: Block leukotrienes that cause airway swelling and mucus production
categories.onset: Within hours; full effect in weeks

medicines.name: Montelukast
medicines.dosage: Adults: 10 mg once daily; Children 2-5 yrs: 4 mg
medicines.use_case: Mild persistent asthma; allergic asthma; exercise-induced

categories.purpose: Reduce severe inflammation during acute attacks or step-up therapy
categories.note: Used short-term for exacerbations; avoid long-term due to side effects

medicines.name: Prednisolone
medicines.dosage: Adults: 30-60 mg/day for 5-7 days; taper as needed

categories.purpose: Target specific immune pathways in severe, refractory asthma
categories.note: For severe uncontrolled asthma not responding to standard therapy

medicines.name: Omalizumab
medicines.use_case: Moderate-severe allergic asthma with elevated IgE

medicines.name: Benralizumab
medicines.dosage: 30 mg every 4 weeks (first 3 doses), then every 8 weeks

categories.purpose: Bronchodilation; adjunct therapy in difficult-to-treat asthma

medicines.name: Theophylline
medicines.use_case: Add-on therapy in severe asthma; useful where inhalers aren't available

medicines.name: Ipratropium Bromide
medicines.use_case: Add-on therapy in acute severe asthma attacks alongside SABA

medicines.name: Tiotropium
medicines.use_case: Add-on therapy in adults with uncontrolled asthma despite ICS/LABA

categories.purpose: Reduce allergic response that triggers asthma
Prevent mast cell degranulation and allergen-triggered airway inflammation

medicines.name: Sodium Cromoglicate (Cromolyn Sodium)
medicines.use_case: Prophylaxis of exercise-induced and allergic asthma
medicines.note: Less commonly used today; no bronchodilatory effect

categories.purpose: Life-saving treatment during severe asthma attacks

medicines.name: Magnesium Sulfate
medicines.use_case: Severe acute asthma not responding to first-line treatment

medicines.name: Helium-Oxygen (Heliox)
medicines.use_case: Reduces work of breathing in critical asthma

Curcumin reduces inflammatory cytokines; natural anti-inflammatory

Magnesium acts as a natural bronchodilator; relaxes airway smooth muscle

Beta-carotene; protects lungs from oxidative damage
Probiotics reduce allergic response and modulate immune system
Probiotic-rich; reduces inflammation and allergic sensitization
Support gut microbiome which is linked to reduced asthma severity
Thins mucus secretions; prevents airway dryness
Soothes airways; anti-inflammatory
Traditional bronchodilatory and anti-inflammatory properties

Can trigger airway constriction via temperature sensitivity
Common food allergens can trigger asthma in sensitized individuals
Histamine causes bronchoconstriction in asthma patients
Food dyes, MSG, and artificial preservatives may trigger attacks

special_dietary_notes: Maintain healthy weight — obesity worsens asthma significantly
Follow Mediterranean diet pattern for best anti-inflammatory outcomes
Avoid known personal food triggers — keep a food diary
Eat small, frequent meals to prevent GERD which can worsen asthma
Do not skip meals; low blood sugar can heighten stress responses

trigger_avoidance: Use air purifiers with HEPA filters at home
Keep windows closed during high pollen seasons
Wash bedding in hot water weekly to eliminate dust mites
Use hypoallergenic pillows and mattress covers
Avoid pet dander — keep pets out of bedroom
Do not smoke and avoid secondhand smoke
Avoid strong perfumes, cleaning chemicals, or aerosols
Wear a scarf or mask in cold weather
Monitor outdoor air quality and avoid going out on high pollution days
Use exhaust fans in kitchen to remove cooking fumes

breathing_exercises.name: Pursed Lip Breathing
breathing_exercises.description: Inhale through nose for 2 counts, exhale slowly through pursed lips for 4 counts
breathing_exercises.benefit: Slows breathing rate; improves gas exchange

breathing_exercises.name: Diaphragmatic Breathing (Belly Breathing)
breathing_exercises.description: Breathe using diaphragm, not chest; belly should rise while inhaling

breathing_exercises.name: Buteyko Breathing Technique
breathing_exercises.description: Controlled slow nasal breathing to reduce over-breathing
breathing_exercises.benefit: Reduces frequency and severity of asthma episodes

breathing_exercises.name: Pranayama (Anulom Vilom / Nadi Shodhana)
breathing_exercises.benefit: Balances nervous system; reduces stress-triggered asthma

recommended: Swimming (warm, humid air is gentle on airways)
precautions: Always carry rescue inhaler during exercise
Use a pre-exercise bronchodilator if prescribed
Warm up for 10 minutes before intense activity
Avoid exercising in cold dry air or high pollen conditions
Monitor breathing and stop if symptoms develop
physical_activity.note: Exercise is beneficial for lung health and weight management. Consult doctor before starting a new exercise program.

mental_health: Practice stress management — stress is a known asthma trigger
Mindfulness meditation and progressive muscle relaxation
Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) for anxiety related to breathlessness
Join asthma support groups for emotional wellbeing
Adequate sleep (7-9 hours) to support immune function

green_zone.symptoms: No symptoms; breathing is good; can do all activities
green_zone.action: Continue regular medications as prescribed. No changes needed.

yellow_zone.symptoms: Cough, wheeze, chest tightness, or shortness of breath; waking at night
yellow_zone.action: Take rescue inhaler (2-4 puffs salbutamol). If no improvement in 20 minutes, repeat. Contact doctor if not improving.

red_zone.symptoms: Severe symptoms; rescue inhaler is not helping; cannot speak in full sentences
red_zone.action: MEDICAL EMERGENCY. Use rescue inhaler immediately. Call emergency services / go to nearest hospital. Do not drive yourself.

complications.description: Prolonged severe asthma attack not responding to bronchodilators. Life-threatening.
Inability to breathe adequately; may require mechanical ventilation.
Lung collapse due to severe air trapping.
Permanent structural changes in airways due to chronic inflammation.
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease features developing alongside asthma (ACOS).
Nocturnal asthma can contribute to obstructive sleep apnea.
Anxiety, depression, and reduced quality of life due to chronic condition.

key_points: Most common chronic disease in children
Symptoms may change with age; some children outgrow asthma
Spacers should be used with MDI inhalers in children under 8
Trigger identification is crucial (pet dander, exercise, infections)
Schools should have asthma action plans on file
Parents and teachers must be educated on recognizing and managing attacks
Poorly controlled asthma is more dangerous than medications during pregnancy
Most asthma medications (ICS, SABA) are considered safe in pregnancy
Monitor asthma carefully — it may worsen in 1/3rd of pregnant women
Avoid oral corticosteroids in first trimester if possible
Inform all healthcare providers about asthma status
Ensure adequate Vitamin D and folate intake
Often underdiagnosed or confused with COPD or heart failure
Age-related muscle weakness affects inhaler technique — use spacers
Higher risk of medication side effects (oral corticosteroids, theophylline)
Multiple comorbidities common (GERD, heart disease, obesity)
Influenza and pneumococcal vaccines strongly recommended

vaccinations_recommended.reason: Respiratory infections are a major trigger; flu can cause severe exacerbations

vaccinations_recommended.frequency: Once (with booster at 65 if given earlier)
vaccinations_recommended.reason: Prevents bacterial pneumonia which can worsen asthma
COVID-19 can trigger severe asthma exacerbations
Whooping cough severely worsens respiratory symptoms

when_to_see_doctor: Waking up at night due to asthma
Rescue inhaler being used more than twice a week
Asthma limiting daily activities or exercise
Peak flow below 80% of personal best for more than 2 days
Any episode requiring emergency room visit
Before starting new medications or making changes to current regimen
emergency_signs: Severe difficulty breathing — unable to speak in full sentences
No relief after 2-3 doses of rescue inhaler
Straining neck or chest muscles to breathe
Silent chest (no wheezing sounds — indicates critical narrowing)

frequently_asked_questions.question: Is asthma curable?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: No, asthma is a chronic condition with no cure. However, with proper medication and lifestyle management, most patients can live normal, active lives with minimal symptoms.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Can children outgrow asthma?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Yes, approximately 50% of children with asthma may experience significant improvement or apparent remission during adolescence. However, asthma can return in adulthood.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Are asthma inhalers safe for long-term use?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Yes, inhaled corticosteroids and other maintenance inhalers are generally safe for long-term use at prescribed doses. The benefits far outweigh the risks of uncontrolled asthma.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Can exercise make asthma worse?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction occurs in many asthma patients, but regular, properly managed exercise is beneficial. Using a rescue inhaler before exercise and warming up properly helps prevent attacks.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Can stress trigger asthma?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Yes. Emotional stress and anxiety cause hyperventilation and can trigger or worsen asthma symptoms. Stress management is an important part of asthma care.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Is asthma hereditary?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Asthma has a genetic component. If one or both parents have asthma or allergies (atopy), the child has a higher risk of developing asthma.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is the difference between a rescue inhaler and a controller inhaler?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: A rescue inhaler (like salbutamol) provides quick relief during an attack by relaxing airway muscles. A controller inhaler (like budesonide) is taken daily to prevent inflammation and reduce attack frequency — it does not provide immediate relief.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Can diet alone control asthma?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: No. Diet is supportive, not curative. A healthy anti-inflammatory diet reduces severity and frequency of episodes, but prescribed medications are essential for asthma control.
